# Interactive add: stage hunks with git add -p

After reading this chapter, you can interactively stage partial file changes using `git add -p`, split large changes into smaller hunks, edit hunk diffs on the fly, and inspect staged versus unstaged work across your repository.

## Staging by hunk instead of file

Standard `git add <file>` is an all-or-nothing operation: it moves every modified line in a file directly into the staging area (the index). When working on complex tasks, developers frequently modify multiple unrelated features, fix typos, or insert temporary debug statements in the exact same file. Committing the entire file forces unrelated edits into a single commit, polluting project history and complicating code reviews.

`git add -p` (short for `--patch`) opens an interactive prompt that splits file modifications into discrete visual sections called **hunks**. For each hunk, Git displays a unified diff and asks what you want to do with those specific lines. By selecting which hunks enter the index, you can craft atomic commits—commits that address exactly one logical fix or feature—without stashing or undoing work in your working directory.

## Mental model

When running patch mode, Git presents diff hunks sequentially, comparing your working tree against the index.

```text
 working tree (local edits)
       │
       ├─► Hunk 1  ──► [ y ] ──► Index (Staged for commit)
       │
       ├─► Hunk 2  ──► [ n ] ──► Remains in Working Tree (Unstaged)
       │
       └─► Hunk 3  ──► [ s ] ──► Split into smaller sub-hunks
```

Selecting `y` (yes) copies only that hunk's changes to the index. Selecting `n` (no) leaves those lines unstaged in your working directory.

## Interactive prompt commands

When `git add -p` launches, Git displays the hunk header (showing line numbers) and diff body, followed by the prompt: `Stage this hunk [y,n,q,a,d,e,?]?`.

Entering `?` shows a help summary of all interactive options:

| Option | Action |
|--------|--------|
| `y` | Stage this hunk for the next commit |
| `n` | Do not stage this hunk; leave it unstaged in the working tree |
| `q` | Quit interactive add; keep all decisions made so far |
| `a` | Stage this hunk and all remaining hunks in this file |
| `d` | Do not stage this hunk or any remaining hunks in this file |
| `g` | Select a hunk to go to by number |
| `/` | Search for a hunk matching the given regex |
| `j` | Leave this hunk undecided and move to the next undecided hunk |
| `k` | Leave this hunk undecided and move to the previous undecided hunk |
| `s` | Split the current hunk into smaller hunks (if empty lines separate changes) |
| `e` | Manually edit the current hunk in your default text editor |

## Lab: staging partial changes

This script sets up a Git repository with a single file `f.txt`, introduces two separate edits, and uses non-interactive `git add -p` filtering (via piped response inputs) to stage only the first edit.

<!-- file: interactive-add-lab.sh -->
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

rm -rf /tmp/git-patch-demo && mkdir /tmp/git-patch-demo && cd /tmp/git-patch-demo
git init -b main
git config user.name "Demo User"
git config user.email "user@example.com"

# Create base file
printf 'line1\nline2\nline3\n' > f.txt
git add f.txt
git commit -m "Initial commit"

# Make multiple edits across the file
printf 'line1\nLINE2\nline3\nline4\n' > f.txt

# Use git add -p non-interactively to answer 'y' to hunk 1 and 'n' to hunk 2
printf "s\ny\nn\n" | git add -p f.txt

# Inspect staged (cached) vs unstaged changes
echo "=== cached ==="
git diff --cached
echo "=== unstaged ==="
git diff
```

Execute the lab script to view the staged and unstaged diffs:

The execution of the lab script generates the diff state shown below.

```text
=== cached ===
diff --git a/f.txt b/f.txt
index 83db48f..534a16e 100644
--- a/f.txt
+++ b/f.txt
@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
 line1
-line2
+LINE2
 line3
=== unstaged ===
diff --git a/f.txt b/f.txt
index 534a16e..f75f249 100644
--- a/f.txt
+++ b/f.txt
@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@
 line1
 LINE2
 line3
+line4
```

Notice the result: line 2's capitalization change (`-line2` / `+LINE2`) is staged in the index (`=== cached ===`), while the addition of `line4` remains unstaged in the working tree (`=== unstaged ===`).

## Splitting and editing hunks

### Splitting hunks (`s`)

Git automatically groups adjacent modified lines into a single hunk. If modified lines are separated by at least one unchanged context line, typing `s` at the prompt causes Git to split the hunk into smaller hunks. Git will then present each smaller hunk individually for decisions.

### Editing hunks (`e`)

When two changes occur on adjacent lines, Git cannot automatically split them with `s`. Typing `e` opens the current diff hunk in the editor configured by `GIT_EDITOR` or `core.editor`.

Within the hunk editor, modify diff prefixes directly to control staging:

- Leave unchanged context lines starting with a space `' '` intact.
- Keep lines starting with `+` to stage them, or delete `+` lines you do not want to stage.
- Keep lines starting with `-` to stage their deletion, or replace `-` with a leading space `' '` to leave those original lines unchanged in the index.

After saving and exiting the editor, Git parses the modified diff and applies it to the index.

## Verification: inspecting partial state

After performing an interactive add, verify your repository state prior to committing using these three standard Git commands:

1. `git status`: Displays files with both staged and unstaged changes under both "Changes to be committed" and "Changes not staged for commit".
2. `git diff --cached`: Shows changes currently staged in the index that will go into the next commit.
3. `git diff`: Shows remaining changes in your working tree that are not yet staged.

To review working tree changes interactively without staging them, run `git diff -p` or `git checkout -p` to discard specific hunks from your working tree.

## Common mistakes

1. **Deleting lines starting with `-` inside `e` (edit mode).** To prevent a deletion from being staged, do not delete the line from the editor buffer; instead, change the leading `-` character to a space `' '`. Deleting a `-` line causes diff hunk context mismatches.
2. **Confusing working tree state with staged state.** After `git add -p`, the working tree file still contains all modifications. Running automated tests against the working tree may pass even if the staged subset is missing critical lines. Always test staged code (e.g., via `git stash -k`) before committing.
3. **Quitting (`q`) expecting unselected hunks to be staged.** Selecting `q` exits interactive mode immediately. All decisions made prior to `q` are saved to the index, but all remaining hunks are left unstaged.

## Summary

- `git add -p` enables hunk-level staging to ensure clean, atomic commits.
- Use `y` to stage a hunk, `n` to skip it, and `s` to split hunks separated by unchanged context lines.
- Use `e` to manually edit adjacent edits within a hunk when automatic splitting is impossible.
- Always check `git diff --cached` and `git diff` after interactive staging to verify the index matches your intended commit scope.
